note: Stated as an absolute. Strict monotonicity across machines needs coordination: either one logical allocator (TiDB's Placement Driver hands out TSO timestamps that 'always move forward and never regress') or special clocks (Spanner's TrueTime gives 'monotonically increasing timestamps' across all servers). Independent, uncoordinated generators can only be roughly ordered.
precise_version: Strictly monotonic IDs across machines need coordination - a single (replicated) timestamp oracle or specially bounded clocks - which costs latency and availability; independent generators can only be roughly ordered.
reason: Agree on imprecise, not on medium. The teacher's design lesson (distributing generation gives up strict order unless you coordinate) is the one interviewers want. TiDB's TSO is itself one logical allocator, i.e. the 'central service' the teacher describes; only Spanner, with TrueTime hardware, is a real exception. A learner who believes the item makes no wrong design decision.

note: Snowflake is only roughly ordered: right. A single MySQL server's auto-increment does allocate unique, increasing values even under the default interleaved lock mode ('guaranteed to be unique and monotonically increasing across all concurrently executing "INSERT-like" statements'), but rolled-back values leave gaps, and a transaction holding a lower ID can commit after one holding a higher ID, so readers can see IDs appear out of order.
precise_version: Snowflake IDs are only roughly time-ordered. A single database's auto-increment hands out unique, increasing values, but concurrent transactions can commit out of ID order and rollbacks leave gaps.
reason: The checker's note says the interleaved mode 'interleaves values across concurrent statements', implying non-monotonic allocation; the MySQL 8.4 page says the opposite (values stay unique and monotonically increasing; only per-statement consecutiveness is lost). What remains is the commit-order caveat, a real but secondary nuance for the student's question, so low rather than medium.
